title: If AI Can Do It Better, Why Am I Still Here? Humanitarian Expertise in the AI Era
html:
If AI Can Do It Better, Why Am I Still Here? Humanitarian Expertise in the AI Era

When Alice Zanni started with me, I gave her an obvious, but hard question that I think many humanitarians have been quietly asking themselves: What is my role in the Generative AI era? How do I ensure that I add value?

Over the past few months, Alice and I worked closely together to explore this question. The result of that effort is our latest report: If AI Can Do It Better, Why Am I Still Here? Humanitarian Expertise in the AI Era.

[PDF download]

Gen AI has transformed how we approach work, yet humanitarian work offers no fixed pathway for individuals to enter the sector. As a result, recognition often relies on peer nomination, credentials and institutional standing. Because Gen AI can produce these outward appearances with ease, defining true expertise must lie outside what a digital system can generate.

We found that true expertise resides in what we call tested participation: the judgement built by making decisions whose consequences come back to you, reading a context nobody has written down, and answering personally for the outcome.

The paper is structured around four central questions:

  • What made me an expert in the first place? It examines how expertise is formed in a sector without fixed pathways, showing that tacit knowledge becomes true judgement through tested participation rather than social labels or peer recognition alone.
  • What is AI changing about my work? It looks at how time saved on administrative drafting can be reallocated to direct contact with affected populations, while also warning against cognitive surrender and the displacement of impartiality decisions.
  • Doesn’t human oversight protect me from this? It challenges the assumption that human sign-off is a sufficient safeguard, demonstrating how reviewer attention erodes under pressure and how complex AI outputs offer less reasoning to check against.
  • What keeps me relevant? It frames the future of the humanitarian practitioner around non-delegable responsibilities, offering concrete guidance for individuals, team leads and institutions to protect critical judgement.

Ultimately, what keeps you relevant is what a system cannot hold on your behalf: judgement built where the consequences reached you, the understanding of context, and the fact that you are the one who answers for the decision.

To preserve this capacity for the future, we must treat entry-level roles as expertise infrastructure rather than overhead. Junior tasks are where judgement is built, and they are the first to be automated. Doing so saves money now against a future cost of the senior judgement needed in the next 10 years.

You can read and download the full report here to explore our complete findings and practical recommendations for practitioners, leaders and policy makers.

Andrej
teaser: Research with Alice Zanni argues that humanitarian expertise rests on tested participation: judgement built by making decisions you answer for, which AI cannot generate.
seo_description: Report by Alice Zanni and Andrej Verity on why true humanitarian expertise lies in tested participation, not credentials AI can imitate, with recommendations for practitioners, leaders and policy makers.
